name: Intercontinental Exchange, Inc.

profile.description: Intercontinental Exchange operates regulated exchanges and clearing houses (including the New York Stock Exchange and ICE Futures, home of the Brent crude benchmark), fixed income and data services, and an end-to-end mortgage technology platform built from the Ellie Mae (2020) and Black Knight (2023) acquisitions. Founded in 2000 by chairman and CEO Jeffrey Sprecher, ICE reported its best third quarter ever in Q3 2026 with $2.8B of net revenue and adjusted EPS of $2.02.

innovation.label: STRONG
innovation.analysis: Innovation Track Record (3/3): ICE has repeatedly redefined itself — from an electronic energy exchange to owner of the NYSE (2013), a data business via Interactive Data (2015), and a mortgage technology platform via Ellie Mae (2020) and Black Knight (2023) — growing revenue from $8.24B in 2020 to $12.64B in 2025 [3][4]. AI Deployment (1/2): Sprecher said in January 2026 that ICE is applying AI models to workflows across the company, and AI voice and chat agents for mortgage servicing are in beta, but no quantified AI revenue or savings has been disclosed [4]. Market Share Leadership (2/2): ICE runs the NYSE, the Brent and global energy futures complex, and the leading U.S. mortgage loan-origination platform; financial futures and options revenue rose 37% and Q3 volume rose 31% YoY [1][5]. Product Pipeline (1/2): Mortgage-servicing AI agents and data products are in development, but without dated revenue targets. R&D Intensity (0/1): ICE does not report R&D as a separate line, so above-peer intensity cannot be shown [3].

inspiration.label: WEAK
inspiration.analysis: Mission Floor (2/4): ICE's stated aim to build and operate digital networks that connect people to opportunity is clear and consistent with its strategy, but is not distinctive among market-infrastructure firms [6]. Community Impact (1/2): ICE publishes annual corporate responsibility reports and the NYSE supports nonprofits through its platform, but no distinctive, dollar-quantified community program was found; Sustainalytics data place ICE in the low ESG-risk category (~19.5) [6][7]. Employee Retention (0/2): No employee turnover or tenure data found; a governance profile notes a long-tenured, compact executive team, but that is leadership rather than workforce retention [4]. Insider Buying (0/2): FMP data show zero open-market insider purchases and 69 insider sales across Q4 2025-Q3 2026 [8].

infrastructure.label: STRONG
infrastructure.analysis: Mechanically scored as a Growth stock (weighted 8.80/10). Profit margin of 38.1%, revenue growth of 14.7% YoY, and forward P/E of 18.9 all score 1.0 [2]. D/E of 80.0% is just above the 70% target (0.96), and ROE of 14.4% is just under 15% (0.96 at 2x weight) [2]. The 5-year revenue CAGR of 8.9% (FMP, $8.24B in 2020 to $12.64B in 2025) scores 0.93 at 2x weight [3]. The weakest metric is the Yahoo-reported PEG of 1.93, which scores 0.54 at 2x weight [2]. Liquidity floor cleared easily: 3.28M shares x $168.85 = ~$554M daily.

ai_resilience.label: MODERATE
ai_resilience.analysis: AI Risk Protection (7/9): ICE's exchanges and clearing houses are regulated, network-effect businesses where liquidity and central counterparty status cannot be replicated by AI tools; heavier AI-driven and algorithmic trading tends to raise volumes, and Q3 2026 volume rose 31% YoY [5]. The Mortgage Technology segment is more exposed, since AI could lower the cost of loan origination and servicing software for competitors, which keeps ICE out of the IMMUNE tier; no analyst commentary found flags AI as a core threat [4]. AI Opportunity (0/1): ICE is deploying AI agents for mortgage servicing (in beta) and internally, but has not disclosed any quantified AI revenue [4].

infinite_game.summary: ICE is a founder-led company whose 26-year arc from energy trading platform to NYSE owner to mortgage digitizer shows real existential flexibility and willingness to make large, long-dated bets. Sinek would credit the consistency of Sprecher's vision of digitizing opaque markets, but would note that the language is about strategy and transactions rather than a cause people sacrifice for, and that competitive framing is about scale and dominance.

just_cause.analysis: Just Cause (2/3): Sprecher's vision of bringing transparency and electronic access to opaque markets — energy, then equities, data, and now the paper-based U.S. mortgage process — has been consistent since the 2000 founding and visibly drives acquisitions [4][6]. It is a genuine, lived purpose, but it reads as a business thesis rather than an idealistic future state that inspires sacrifice, so it falls short of 3.

trusting_teams.analysis: Trusting Teams (1/2): ICE has a long-tenured, compact executive team under a founder who has led since 2000, which gives organizational stability [4]. No evidence of exceptional empowerment, low turnover, or psychological-safety practices was found, and the combined CEO/chair role concentrates authority.

worthy_rivals.analysis: Worthy Rivals (0/1): ICE's competitive posture with CME, Nasdaq, and mortgage-software rivals has been expressed through acquisitions that remove competitors (for example Ellie Mae and Black Knight) rather than through language about learning from rivals [3][4]. No evidence of an infinite competitive mindset was found.

existential_flexibility.analysis: Existential Flexibility (2/2): ICE has fundamentally reinvented itself more than once — from an OTC energy platform to the owner of the NYSE in 2013, then into data services and, with the Ellie Mae and Black Knight deals, into a mortgage technology business that now sits alongside the exchange franchise [4]. Each pivot entered a new market rather than extending the old one.

courage_to_lead.analysis: Courage to Lead (2/2): Management closed the Ellie Mae acquisition during the 2020 COVID crisis and then pursued Black Knight, accepting years of dilutive integration and heavy debt to build a mortgage platform whose payoff depends on a long-term housing cycle [3][4]. Combined with the earlier NYSE purchase, this is a pattern of choosing long-term capability over near-term earnings.

investment_thesis: ICE is a high-margin compounder that just posted the best third quarter in its history: $2.8B of net revenue, net income of $940M, GAAP EPS of $1.67, and adjusted EPS of $2.02, with financial futures and options revenue up 37% and total Q3 volume up 31% YoY [1][5]. Revenue has grown from $8.24B (2020) to $12.64B (2025) with diluted EPS rising from $3.77 to $5.77, and the business earns a 38% net margin with a forward P/E of 18.9 [2][3]. Volatility in rates and energy drives exchange volumes, while data and mortgage technology add recurring revenue that smooths the cycle.
thesis_continued: The bear case centers on leverage and mortgage exposure. Total debt of ~$24B against $936M cash (D/E 80%) reflects the Black Knight purchase, and ROE of 14.4% remains below the 15% hurdle [2]. Mortgage Technology depends on a housing-origination recovery that has repeatedly been pushed out, and AI-native loan software could compress pricing. Exchange revenue is also cyclical: the 31% volume surge driven by interest-rate contracts could normalize, and the 1.93 PEG means the stock is not cheap relative to expected growth [2][5].
key_catalysts: Sustained rate and energy volatility — Q3 2026 volume up 31% YoY and financial futures and options revenue up 37%, with interest-rate contracts driving the gain [1][5]
Mortgage origination recovery — a lower-rate refinancing cycle would lift transaction revenue on the Encompass and Black Knight platforms built from the Ellie Mae and Black Knight acquisitions [4]
Deleveraging and capital return — strong free cash flow from a 38% net-margin business can pay down Black Knight debt and grow the dividend ($2.08 annual rate) [2]
key_risks: Mortgage technology stagnation — prolonged high mortgage rates keep origination volumes depressed and delay returns on the Ellie Mae and Black Knight investments [4]
Volume normalization — the 31% Q3 volume spike was rate-driven and could reverse if macro volatility fades, pressuring exchange revenue [5]
Leverage — ~$24B of total debt (D/E 80%) limits flexibility for further acquisitions and exposes earnings to refinancing costs [2]
